source_text: εὐλογήσαι σε κύριος καὶ φυλάξαι σε, ἐπιφάναι κύριος τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἐπί σε καὶ ἐλεήσαι σε, ἐπάραι κύριος τὸ πρόσωπον αὐτοῦ ἐπί σε καὶ δῴη σοι εἰρήνην». 18.5 ἵνα δηλώσῃ τρία πρόσωπα, οὐκ εἶπεν ἅπαξ· «κύριος εὐλογήσαι σε καὶ ἐπιφάναι σοι καὶ δῴη σοι εἰρήνην», ἀλλὰ τρίτον ὠνόμασεν «κύριον». 18.6 Καὶ ὣς ἡνίκα προφητεύουσιν Ἀγγαῖος μὲν θεόχρηστον ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ πατρὸς φέρων φωνὴν οὕτως ἔχουσαν· «ἴσχυε, Ζοροβάβελ, διότι ἐγὼ μεθ' ὑμῶν εἰμι· καὶ ὁ λόγος μου ὁ ἀγαθὸς καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα μου ἐν μέσῳ ὑμῶν»· 18.7 Ἠσαΐας δὲ ἐξ ὁμοτίμων τῶν αὐτοτελῶν ὑποστάσεων ὁμότιμον τὴν ἀποστολὴν γεγενῆσθαι λέγων καὶ ἐν ὀλίγῃ ῥήσει πᾶσαν κοινωνίαν αὐτῶν ἐνδεικνύμενος καὶ βοῶν· «καὶ νῦν κύριος κύριος ἀπέσταλκέν με καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ». 18.8 οὐ γὰρ ἁπλῶς δεύτερον ὠνόμασεν «κύριος κύριος» καὶ οὕτω «τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ», ἀλλ' ἵνα καὶ τὰς ὑποστάσεις καὶ τὴν μίαν δηλώσῃ θεότητα καὶ θέλησιν. 18.9 ∆αυῒδ δέ καὶ γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς ἀρήγει τῷ τοιῷδε κεφαλαίῳ καὶ ᾠδῆς ἔμπλεα πάντα ποιεῖ καὶ ἐκφαίνει, ὅπῃ πίστεως ἔσχεν κατὰ τάσδε τὰς λέξεις· ἐν μὲν ιζʹ ψαλμῷ· «τίς θεὸς πάρεξ τοῦ κυρίου καὶ τίς θεὸς πλὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν; ὁ θεὸς ὁ περι ζωννύων με δύναμιν»· 18.10 ἐν δὲ νηʹ· «σὺ ὁ θεὸς ἀντιλήπτωρ μου εἶ. ὁ θεός μου, τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ αὐτοῦ προφθάσει με. ὁ θεός μου δείξει μοι ἐν τοῖς ἐχθροῖς μου». 18.11 ἐν δὲ ϟεʹ· «ᾄσατε τῷ κυρίῳ ᾆσμα καινόν, ᾄσατε τῷ κυρίῳ, πᾶσα ἡ γῆ, ᾄσατε τῷ κυρίῳ, εὐλογήσατε τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ». 18.12 τρίτον γὰρ ὀνομάσας ἢ κύριον ἢ θεὸν τὴν τριάδα παρεδήλωσεν. 18.13 Ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἅννα εἰς τὰς βασιλείας προσευχομένη τὴν τριάδα ἐπεκαλέσατο εἰποῦσα· «ἀδωναί, κύριε, ἐλωεὶ σαβαώθ». 18.14 ἑρμηνεύεται γὰρ τῇ ἑβραΐδι φωνῇ τὸ «ἀδωναί»· κύριος· καὶ πάλιν ἑλλάδι φωνῇ εἶπεν «κύριος». καὶ τρίτον ἑβραϊστὶ ἔφη «ἐλωεὶ σαβαώθ», ὅπερ ἐστί· θεὲ στρατιῶν ἤτοι δυνάμεων. 18.15 ἤδη δὲ νῦν καὶ Ἠλίας ὁ Θεσβίτης ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν βασιλειῶν ἱστορίᾳ, τῆς Σιδωνίας χήρας τὸν υἱὸν νεκρὸν ὄντα ἀναβιῶναι εὐξάμενος, τρίτον ἐνεφύσησεν εἰς αὐτὸν καὶ οὕτως ἀνέστησεν, 18.16 ἐκ τούτου μονονουχὶ σημάνας, ὡς αὐτὸς ἐν τῇ προσευχῇ τὴν ζωοποιὸν ἐπεκαλέσατο τριάδα, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἡμᾶς μὴ ἄλλως πιστεύειν καὶ δοξάζειν διδάξας. 18.17 Καὶ τοῖς ὑδροφόροις δὲ παρακελευόμενος «δισσεύσατε» καί «τρισσεύσατε», τὰς τρεῖς πανυμνήτους ὑποστάσεις ἰσοδυνάμως καὶ ὁμοτίμως πανταχοῦ ἐν πᾶσιν ἐνεργεῖν παρεδήλου. 18.18 Εἰ δὲ βούλεσθε, γνώριμον ὑμῖν καὶ ἐκ θείας φωνῆς αὖθις τὸ κινούμενον ποιήσω. 18.19 ἐν γὰρ βίβλῳ γενέσεως, ἐν τῇ πυργοποιΐᾳ ὁ θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ τὰς μακαρίας ὑποστάσεις ἐξέφηνεν πρὸς τὸν ἑαυτοῦ υἱὸν καὶ τὸ ἅγιον αὐτοῦ πνεῦμα εἰρηκώς· «δεῦτε καταβάντες συγχέωμεν ἐκεῖ αὐτῶν τὰς γλώσσας, ἵνα μὴ ἀκούσωσιν ἕκαστος τὴν φωνὴν τοῦ πλησίον». 18.20 Καὶ Μωϋσῆς δὲ τὴν ἰσότητα τῆς τριάδος, ὡς οἶμαι, δηλῶν ἐξέθετο μίαν ἄμπελον ἐν τρισὶ 18 πυθμέσι, τοῦτον τοῦ ἄλλου πυθμένος οὐδαμοῦ προβαθέστερον εἰρηκώς, ἵνα μή τις τὴν ὑπόστασιν ταύτην ἐκείνης προτερεύειν νομίσῃ, ἀλλὰ τὰς τρεῖς ἐν μιᾷ συντείνειν θεότητι πάντες πιστεύωμεν. 18.21 ∆ιὰ τοῦτο καὶ ἡ θεόπνευστος γραφὴ ἐκώλυσεν ἐν τῷ θυσιαστηρίῳ, ἐν ᾧ ἡ τριὰς δοξάζεται, ἀναβαθμοὺς ποιεῖν, ὥστε μὴ ὡς ἐν βαθμοῖς διορίζεσθαι ἀνθρώπους καθ' ὕφεσίν τινα εἶναι τὰς θείας ὑποστάσεις. 18.22 Καὶ ἁπλῶς ἡ παλαιὰ διαθήκη τύπον φέρουσα τῆς νέας μυστικῶς καὶ προμηθεστάτως διαλέγεται, αἰνιττομένη μᾶλλον ἐν πολλοῖς ἢ φράζουσα ἐν ταὐτῷ· καὶ φράζουσα πλέον ἤπερ αἰνισσομένη τὸ ὕστερον ἐκφανθὲν μυστήριον, ὅπως μήτε πλήξῃ τῇ ἀθρόᾳ προσβολῇ τοὺς ἀμυήτους καὶ οὔπω ὄντας σταθερούς τε καὶ δεκτικοὺς τῆς θεοπτίας, μήτε μὴν εἰς τὸ παντελὲς ζημιώσῃ· 18.23 τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἦν ἀπειρίας, τὸ δὲ ἀπανθρωπίας. 18.24 πολλάκις δὲ καὶ ἅπερ τυχὸν ἐνταῦθα ἡμῖν δυσεφίκτως ἔφρασεν,
pass_a_gloss: [...] 'may the Lord bless you and guard you, may the Lord make his face appear upon you and have mercy on you, may the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace'. 18.5 In order to make plain three persons, he did not say once: 'may the Lord bless you and appear to you and give you peace', but named 'Lord' a third time. 18.6 And thus, when they prophesy: Haggai on the one hand, bearing a God-given voice from the person of the Father that runs thus: 'be strong, Zerubbabel, because I am with you; and my good word and my Spirit are in the middle of you'; 18.7 Isaiah on the other hand, saying that the sending has come about equal in honour from hypostases equal in honour and complete in themselves, and in a brief utterance pointing out their whole communion, and crying aloud: 'and now the Lord, the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit'. 18.8 For not idly did he name a second time 'Lord, Lord', and so 'his Spirit', but so that he might make plain both the hypostases and the one Godhead and will. 18.9 And David: for he too lends aid to this sort of chief article, and makes all things full of song, and shows forth how he stood in faith, according to these words: in Psalm seventeen [Greek numbering]: 'who is God except the Lord, and who is God besides our God? the God who girds me round with power'; 18.10 and in fifty-eight: 'you, O God, are my helper. My God, his mercy (his) will go before me. My God will show me among my enemies'; 18.11 and in ninety-five: 'sing to the Lord a new song, sing to the Lord, all the earth, sing to the Lord, bless his name'. 18.12 For by naming either Lord or God a third time he indicated the Trinity. 18.13 But Hannah too, praying in the Kingdoms, called upon the Trinity, saying: 'Adonai, Lord, Eloi Sabaoth'. 18.14 For in the Hebrew tongue 'Adonai' is interpreted: Lord; and again in the Greek tongue she said 'Lord'; and a third time in Hebrew she said 'Eloi Sabaoth', which is: O God of hosts, or of powers. 18.15 And now also Elijah the Tishbite, in the third history of the Kingdoms, having prayed that the son of the Sidonian widow, who was dead, come back to life, breathed into him a third time and so raised him up, 18.16 by this all but signalling that he himself in his prayer called upon the life-making Trinity, and also teaching us not to believe and glorify otherwise. 18.17 And in urging the water-carriers 'do it twice' and 'do it thrice', he was indicating that the three all-hymned hypostases work with equal power and equal honour everywhere in all things. 18.18 And if you wish, I will make the matter under discussion known to you again also from a divine voice. 18.19 For in the book of Genesis, at the tower-building, the God and Father disclosed the blessed hypostases, having said to his own Son and his Holy Spirit: 'come, having gone down let us confuse their tongues there, so that they may not hear, each one, the voice of the neighbour'. 18.20 And Moses too, making plain, as I think, the equality of the Trinity, set out one vine on three stocks, having said nowhere that this stock was set deeper than the other stock, so that no one might think this hypostasis to come before that one, but that we all might believe the three to be drawn together in one Godhead. 18.21 On account of this also the God-breathed Scripture forbade making steps at the altar, at which the Trinity is glorified, so that people might not define, as on steps, the divine hypostases to be by some lowering. 18.22 And simply, the old covenant, bearing a type of the new, converses mystically and most providently, hinting rather in many places than declaring in the same place; and declaring more than hinting the mystery revealed later, so that it might neither strike with a massed assault the uninitiated and those not yet steady and receptive of the vision of God, nor indeed bring loss to the uttermost; 18.23 for the one was a mark of inexperience, the other of inhumanity. 18.24 And often also the things which perhaps it expressed to us here in a hard-to-reach way, [...]
pass_b_english: … “May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine upon you and have mercy on you; may the Lord lift up his face upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24-26). To show three Persons, he did not say once, “May the Lord bless you and shine upon you and give you peace”; he named “Lord” three times.

So it is too when Haggai and Isaiah prophesy. Haggai brings a voice given by God, spoken in the person of the Father, which runs thus: “Be strong, Zerubbabel, for I am with you; and my good word and my Spirit are in your midst” (Haggai 2:4-5). Isaiah says that the sending came, equal in honour, from hypostases equal in honour and complete in themselves; in one brief saying he points out their whole communion, and he cries: “And now the Lord, the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16). It was not idly that he named the Lord twice, “Lord, Lord”, and then “his Spirit”: he meant to show both the hypostases and the one Godhead and will.

And David too: for he also comes to the aid of this article of faith, fills everything with song, and shows in these words where he stood in faith. In Psalm 18: “Who is God but the Lord, and who is God besides our God? It is God who girds me with power” (Psalm 18:31-32). In Psalm 59: “You, O God, are my helper. My God, his mercy will go before me. My God will show me among my enemies” (Psalm 59:9-10). In Psalm 96: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth; sing to the Lord, bless his name” (Psalm 96:1-2). By naming “Lord” or “God” three times he pointed to the Trinity.

Hannah too, praying in the Book of Kingdoms, called upon the Trinity when she said, “Adonai, Lord, Eloi Sabaoth” (1 Samuel 1:11). In the Hebrew tongue “Adonai” means “Lord”; then she said “Lord” again in Greek; and a third time, in Hebrew, she said “Eloi Sabaoth”, that is, “O God of hosts”, or “of powers”.

And now Elijah the Tishbite too, in the third book of the history of the Kingdoms, prayed that the son of the widow of Sidon, who was dead, might come back to life; he breathed into him three times and so raised him up (1 Kings 17:21). By this he all but declared that he himself had called upon the life-giving Trinity in his prayer, and he taught us as well to believe and to glorify in no other way. And when he urged the water-carriers, “Do it a second time” and “Do it a third time” (1 Kings 18:34), he was showing that the three all-praised hypostases act everywhere and in all things with equal power and equal honour.

If you wish, I will make the matter in hand known to you once more, from a divine voice as well. In the book of Genesis, at the building of the tower, God the Father disclosed the blessed hypostases when he said to his own Son and to his Holy Spirit: “Come, let us go down and confuse their tongues there, so that each may not understand the voice of his neighbour” (Genesis 11:7).

Moses too, as I think, showing the equality of the Trinity, set forth one vine on three stocks (Genesis 40:10), and nowhere said that one stock ran deeper than another. So no one should suppose that this hypostasis comes before that one; rather, we should all believe that the three are joined together in one Godhead.

That is why the God-inspired Scripture forbade making steps up to the altar (Exodus 20:26), the altar at which the Trinity is glorified: so that people should not, as though on steps, define the divine hypostases as standing in some order of descent.

In short, the Old Testament, bearing a type of the New, speaks in mysteries and with the greatest forethought. In many places it hints rather than declaring everything in one place; and yet it declares, more than it hints, the mystery that was revealed later. It does this so that it may neither strike the uninitiated, those not yet steady or able to receive the vision of God, with a sudden onslaught, nor yet leave them wholly deprived. The first would have shown want of skill, the second want of humanity. And often, too, the things it perhaps expressed to us here in a way hard to grasp …

hard to reach, hard to grasp

choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English turned Ἀγγαῖος into 'a Persian prophet' and left 18.6-18.7 as a fragment with no main clause; turned 18.7 into 'his mission has become similar to the similar ones'; 18.9 ἀρήγει τῷ τοιῷδε κεφαλαίῳ into 'rises by such a heading'; made Hannah 'he' and had her 'praying toward the kingdoms'; cut Elijah's sentence in two at 'And now also Elijah... / The Thessian'; rendered συγχέωμεν 'let us pour out'; made 18.21 say the hypostases might be 'defined as being men'; and in 18.22-18.23 gave 'in anticipation' for προμηθεστάτως, 'the unhearing' for ἀμυήτους and 'infinity' for ἀπειρίας (here: want of skill). It also had a bracket filler [him]. References: Haggai 2:4 widened to 2:4-5 (the words 'my Spirit in your midst' are verse 5); Psalm 18:31-32, Psalm 59:9-10, Psalm 96:1-2, 1 Kings 17:21, 1 Kings 18:34, Genesis 40:10 and Exodus 20:26 added.

choices.english: … “May the Lord bless you … give you peace”
choices.why: The section opens inside the quotation begun in the previous section ('Thus you shall bless Israel:'). Only the blessing this section holds is translated, with a leading ellipsis.

choices.term: Καὶ ὣς ἡνίκα προφητεύουσιν Ἀγγαῖος μέν … Ἠσαΐας δέ …
choices.english: So it is too when Haggai and Isaiah prophesy. Haggai brings … Isaiah says …
choices.why: The Greek period has no main verb after ἡνίκα: two participle clauses (Haggai … φέρων; Isaiah … λέγων … βοῶν) and then 18.8 begins with γάρ. English names the two subjects and gives each its own sentence, so nothing is added and the sentence is not left broken.

choices.english: spoken in the person of the Father
choices.why: Prosopological reading: the prophet speaks as the Father's mouthpiece.

choices.term: ἐξ ὁμοτίμων τῶν αὐτοτελῶν ὑποστάσεων ὁμότιμον τὴν ἀποστολήν
choices.english: the sending came, equal in honour, from hypostases equal in honour and complete in themselves
choices.why: Didymus reads 'the Lord … and his Spirit' as joint senders of the prophet; ὁμότιμος is kept as 'equal in honour' in both places.
Didymus' technical term for each of the Three, set beside πρόσωπον (Person) in 18.5; kept as a technical word rather than flattened into 'person'.
Didymus numbers the Psalms by the Greek Bible: LXX 17 = Psalm 18 (verses 31-32), LXX 58 = Psalm 59 (verses 9-10), LXX 95 = Psalm 96 (verses 1-2). English numbers are used in the text.

choices.english: praying in the Book of Kingdoms
choices.why: τὰς βασιλείας is the Greek Bible's name for the books of Samuel and Kings (1 Kingdoms = 1 Samuel), not 'kingdoms' as a direction.

choices.term: ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν βασιλειῶν ἱστορίᾳ … τρίτον ἐνεφύσησεν
choices.english: in the third book of the history of the Kingdoms … he breathed into him three times
choices.why: 3 Kingdoms = 1 Kings. The Greek of 1 Kings 17:21 reads 'he breathed into the child three times' where the Hebrew (and KJV) has 'stretched himself upon the child'; Didymus' argument rests on the Greek.

choices.english: “Do it a second time” and “Do it a third time”
choices.why: Elijah's command on Carmel to pour water on the altar, 1 Kings 18:34.

choices.term: μίαν ἄμπελον ἐν τρισὶ πυθμέσι … οὐδαμοῦ προβαθέστερον εἰρηκώς
choices.english: one vine on three stocks … and nowhere said that one stock ran deeper than another
choices.why: The cupbearer's dream in Genesis 40:10 ('three stocks' in the Greek). οὐδαμοῦ goes with εἰρηκώς: Moses nowhere said it; Didymus argues from silence.

choices.english: standing in some order of descent
choices.why: ὕφεσις is a lowering in rank; the steps image of Exodus 20:26 is carried through.

choices.term: αἰνιττομένη μᾶλλον ἐν πολλοῖς ἢ φράζουσα ἐν ταὐτῷ
choices.english: In many places it hints rather than declaring everything in one place
choices.why: ἐν πολλοῖς is set against ἐν ταὐτῷ: the Old Testament scatters hints rather than stating the mystery in one place.

choices.term: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἦν ἀπειρίας, τὸ δὲ ἀπανθρωπίας
choices.english: The first would have shown want of skill, the second want of humanity
choices.why: ἀπειρία here is inexperience (an unskilled teacher overwhelms beginners), not infinity; ἀπανθρωπία answers 'leave them wholly deprived'.

choices.term: ἅπερ τυχὸν ἐνταῦθα ἡμῖν δυσεφίκτως ἔφρασεν,
choices.english: And often, too, the things it perhaps expressed to us here in a way hard to grasp …
choices.why: The section ends mid-sentence; the thought continues in the next section. Ends with '…'.
A word split by a line break in the copy-text is read as one word; the printed number 18 inside 18.20 is page debris and is skipped.
